## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects… [truncated]

# Linda Mungai — Applied Performance Specialist
## Project Plan aligned to ICE Form I-983 (STEM OPT Training Plan)

**CONFIDENTIAL — restricted circulation.** Immigration status detail in this document
was shared in a closed staff meeting on 2026-08-19 with an explicit instruction to keep
it inside that room. Known to: Chris Ruf, Kenny Boyd, Megan (HR), her sport coaches,
Eric Rash. Do not forward, do not post to Teams, do not put in a shared channel.

Prepared: 2026-08-19
Prepared by: Eric Rash, Director of Applied Performance (supervisor of record on the I-983)
Sources: ICE Form I-983 pp. 3 & 5 (`XXXX_Transfer/LindaICE.pdf`); Ruf/Rash planning call
2026-07-30; Applied Performance planning call 2026-07-09; staff meeting 2026-08-19.

---

## 1. Why this plan exists

The I-983 is the spine, not the meeting notes. It is a signed federal training plan, and
Linda must file periodic progress evaluations against it. Chris Ruf said it plainly on
2026-08-19: *"she shared that document with me. So we'll just tailor her work to that,
just so it's easy for her to fill out."*

So every project below is written as a row with the same five columns:

| Column | Question it answers |
|---|---|
| **Objective** | What gets built |
| **First step** | What happens in week one |
| **Tools** | Which I-983-named technology it uses |
| **Neuroscience / analytics tie** | Why this counts against a neuroscience degree |
| **Evidence artifact** | What she can name in the ICE evaluation box |
| **Route** | How it gets in front of a coach without dying |

The **evidence artifact** column is the whole point. A thin evaluation at the 12-month
mark is the real failure mode here, and it is entirely preventable by deciding now what
each project leaves behind on paper.

### What the form actually commits her to

From I-983 p. 3, Student Role and Goals & Objectives:

- **Title:** Applied Performance Specialist. **Degree of record:** Neuroscience.
- **Technologies named:** VALD force plates, GPS systems, velocity-based training
  devices, heart rate monitors, timing systems, "related sport science tools."
- **Analytical skills named:** Excel **and Python**, statistical tools, performance
  trend identification, evidence-based decision support.
- **Domains named:** training load, fatigue, recovery status, adaptation, and
  explicitly *"neuromuscular and cognitive demands"* — how the nervous system responds
  to training stress, fatigue, and adaptation.
- **Supervision named:** Director of Applied Performance, via *regularly scheduled
  meetings* reviewing ongoing projects, data collection, and analysis; all analytical
  outputs and recommendations reviewed by the supervisor before informing training
  decisions.

That last line is a commitment on **your** calendar, not just hers. See §6.

---

## 2. Timeline anchors

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| **2026-09-02** | Professional development / interview prep series starts (alternating weeks) |
| **Sept 2026** | Projects 1 and 2 run — data collection window while tennis is in-season prep |
| **~Oct–Nov 2026** | OPT decision expected ("next two to three months" as of 2026-08-19) |
| **On approval** | Two-year clock starts |
| **12 months from OPT start** | First self-evaluation due (I-983 p. 5, block 1) |
| **End of period** | Final evaluation due (I-983 p. 5, block 2) |

> **Verify the evaluation due dates with the Baylor DSO / ISSS.** The form carries two
> evaluation blocks and the standard cadence is a 12-month self-evaluation plus a final,
> but the exact dates key off her authorized start date, which is not on the pages we
> have. Do not guess this one.

---

## 3. Core projects — women's tennis

Both Ruf and you independently landed on per-athlete performance profiles as the
starting point. That sequence is settled; it is not re-opened here.

### Project 1 — Women's tennis performance profiles

| | |
|---|---|
| **Objective** | A per-athlete neuromuscular profile for every woman on the roster |
| **First step** | Lock the test battery and the testing dates before touching an athlete. Battery: VALD force plates (CMJ), ForceFrame (hip/groin strength), NordBord (hamstring). Confirm which of these are on-hand and calibrated. |
| **Tools** | VALD force plates, ForceFrame, NordBord |
| **Neuroscience / analytics tie** | Force-time curve variables *are* neuromuscular output — RSI-mod, contraction time, asymmetry. This is the cleanest possible mapping of "neuromuscular function" from the form to real work. |
| **Evidence artifact** | A written testing protocol document + a completed profile sheet per athlete. Both are nameable in the ICE box. |
| **Route** | Small squad, low friction. As long as Joey's big rocks are checked off, extra testing is not a hassle. Blair (new assistant coach) is the liaison — she already pushed the high/low change through. |

**Watch-out:** lock the metric definitions and the test protocol *before* the first
session. If the battery changes mid-year, every across-time comparison becomes
artifactual and the profile is worthless. This is a one-way door.

---

### Project 2 — Normative ranges

| | |
|---|---|
| **Objective** | Baylor women's tennis normative ranges, benchmarked against the wider collegiate landscape |
| **First step** | Request the collegiate comparison dataset from VALD. Ruf flagged VALD as the source; the ask should go out before the profiles are complete so the data is waiting. |
| **Tools** | VALD normative data; **Excel and Python** for the analysis |
| **Neuroscience / analytics tie** | This is the Python requirement from the form, discharged. Descriptive distributions, percentile banding, within-athlete variability. |
| **Evidence artifact** | A normative range reference sheet + the analysis script. A script in a repo is unusually strong evidence of "data analysis skills developed through statistical tools such as Excel and Python." |
| **Route** | Internal first. Do not present ranges to a coach until the noise floor is known — see below. |

**Ordering rule, non-negotiable:** establish the typical error (noise floor) of each test
*before* interpreting whether any athlete's value is meaningfully high or low. A
normative band that ignores measurement error produces confident nonsense. Use
`tools/reliability.py` in AgentAssist for TE and SWC rather than reasoning about it in
prose. This is also a genuinely good teaching moment for her.

---

### Project 3 — Tennis-specific conditioning test (R&D)

This is the flagship. Ruf wants it usable on the men's side too.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Objective** | Design, present, pilot, and evaluate a tennis-specific conditioning test |
| **First step** | Literature review only. Models and attempts already exist — she finds them, summarizes them, and rates them for feasibility here. No test design until the review is done. |
| **Tools** | **Heart rate monitors, timing systems/gates** — the two I-983 technologies otherwise uncovered by this plan. Build them in deliberately. |
| **Neuroscience / analytics tie** | Fatigue and recovery response; cardiovascular vs. neuromuscular demand. Pair the test with a pre/post force plate jump to read neuromuscular fatigue against cardiovascular load — that pairing is the neuroscience angle, and it is genuinely interesting work. |
| **Evidence artifact** | Three separate artifacts, and this is why it is the flagship: (1) a written literature review, (2) a test protocol with a reliability plan, (3) a pilot results report. Three-stage projects fill an evaluation box on their own. |
| **Route** | **Present to staff before Joey.** Ruf's read is that Joey will ignore it anyway, so the value is the exercise and the insight, not adoption. Frame it that way to her up front so a shrug from Joey doesn't read as failure. Blair carries it in. Dr. Kovacs is already a supportive voice on the high/low model and is worth a second conversation. |

**Reliability first here too.** A conditioning test with unknown typical error cannot
detect change. The test-retest plan is part of the protocol, not an afterthought.

---

### Project 4 — Match profiles

| | |
|---|---|
| **Objective** | Connect on-court match demand to weight-room and cardiovascular metrics |
| **First step** | Find out what match data actually exists and is accessible. This is a feasibility check, not a build. If the data is not there, the project does not start. |
| **Tools** | Match data; **GPS** if court-side use is viable; force plate and conditioning outputs from Projects 1 and 3 |
| **Neuroscience / analytics tie** | External load vs. internal response — the holistic athlete picture you described. Also the "cognitive demands" language in the form, if match context is included. |
| **Evidence artifact** | A holistic athlete report per player, integrating three data streams |
| **Route** | Last. Depends on 1 and 3 existing first. |

**Flag:** this is the most likely project to stall on data access. Treat it as the
stretch goal, not a commitment. Better to finish three projects well than four thinly.

---

## 4. Ongoing threads (run alongside, not sequenced)

**Load monitoring and wellness — women's tennis.** Ruf's original framing: *"what can
she do to help build out some load monitoring or wellness pieces for them."* The high/low
model is already partly won — Monday/Wednesday/Friday dense work, Tuesday/Thursday regen
and mobility, and the athletes gave good feedback in the last weeks of summer. Her job is
to instrument what is already happening, not to re-litigate the model. Simple wellness
capture + session RPE is enough to start.

**Athlete education programming.** Assist role. Low cost, high visibility, and it maps to
the form's "communicating findings effectively with coaching and sports medicine staff."
Give her one topic to own end-to-end rather than a supporting role on five.

---

## 5. Duties — workload, not I-983 projects

Keep these in a separate bucket. They are real work and they consume real hours, but they
are **not** evidence for the training plan. Listing them together is how the "keep her
busy, not burn her out" line gets enforced — this column is the one that quietly fills up.

| Duty | Notes |
|---|---|
| Lead on staff onboarding | She is *lead*, not assist |
| SCCC exam prep — assist Coach Winger | "May have a chance to have Linda on that this year" — confirm |
| Community service — assist Coach Javi | |
| Women's tennis schedule into TeamUp | She owns it; already has the schedule |
| Men's tennis coverage while Coach Hobby travels | Recurring, unpredictable |
| Biweekly applied performance staff meetings | Ruf: she needs to be in these |

**Load check:** that is five recurring duties plus four projects. Something has to give,
and the honest answer is Project 4. Say so out loud rather than letting it fail quietly.

---

## 6. Your obligations under the form

The I-983 puts commitments on the supervisor, not only the student. Page 3 specifies:

1. **Regularly scheduled supervision meetings** reviewing ongoing projects, data
   collection, and analysis. Put a recurring 30-minute slot on the calendar now. The
   biweekly applied performance staff meeting does not satisfy this — the form describes
   direct supervision, not group attendance.
2. **Review of all analytical outputs before they inform training decisions.** Nothing
   she produces goes to a coach unreviewed. This is also good practice regardless.
3. **Sign both evaluation blocks** on p. 5 as "Employer Official with Signatory
   Authority" — confirm that is you and not Kenny or Chris.
4. **Keep a running log.** Two lines after each supervision meeting. At month 12 you will
   be reconstructing a year from memory otherwise, and that is where thin evaluations
   come from.

---

## 7. Coverage check against the I-983 technology list

| Named in the form | Covered by | Status |
|---|---|---|
| VALD force plates | Projects 1, 2, 3 | Strong |
| Velocity-based training devices | Weight-room work, load monitoring | Adequate — could be stronger |
| Heart rate monitors | Project 3 | Covered *only if* Project 3 runs |
| Timing systems | Project 3 | Covered *only if* Project 3 runs |
| GPS systems | Project 4 | **Weak** — Project 4 is the stretch goal |
| Excel | Projects 1, 2 | Strong |
| **Python** | Project 2 | Covered *only if* she writes the analysis herself |

**Two real gaps.** GPS and Python both hang off single projects, and one of those
projects is the one most likely to be cut.

Fixes, in order of ease:
- **Python:** make it explicit that she writes the Project 2 analysis, not that she is
  handed a spreadsheet. Cheapest fix available and it strengthens the strongest project.
- **GPS:** give her a defined touchpoint in the football or soccer GPS workflow — even a
  scoped, read-only analysis piece — so it does not depend on Project 4 surviving.
- **VBT:** one small piece of load-velocity profiling inside the tennis weight-room work
  would firm this up cheaply.

---

## 8. Data privacy — applies to her too

Athlete data is FERPA-covered and possibly HIPAA-covered, and it is **not** covered by
Baylor's AI approval. The rule that applies to your tooling applies to her work:

- Deterministic scripts, spreadsheets, and local analysis on identifiable athlete data:
  **fine**.
- Pasting rosters, athlete names, or identifiable performance data into any AI prompt:
  **not fine**.

Cover this in her first supervision meeting. She is new to the department and this is not
an obvious rule.

---

## 9. Open items — confirm before assigning

1. **Connexon integration analysis with volleyball.** The 2026-08-19 transcript is
   ambiguous — the "her" may refer to Blair, not Linda. **Confirm with Ruf before this
   goes on her plate.**
2. **SCCC exam prep involvement** — stated as a "may," not a commitment.
3. **Evaluation due dates** — confirm with the DSO (§2).
4. **Signatory authority** — confirm whether you or Kenny signs p. 5.
5. **Coach authority.** Kenny Boyd, 2026-07-09: *"she's going to need somebody with
   authority to champion her work with the teams that she works with… it's gonna come
   from Chris and myself. Not even necessarily you."* When a coach conversation needs
   weight behind it, escalate to Chris or Kenny. That is not a failure on your part — it
   is the arrangement they set.

---

## 10. Document gap

`LindaICE.pdf` contains **pages 3 and 5 only** of a 5-page form. Pages 1, 2, and 4 are
missing. If this copy is needed for filing or for the evaluations, get the complete form.

---

## First three moves

1. **Schedule the recurring supervision meeting.** It is a form requirement and it is
   the thing most likely to be skipped.
2. **Send the VALD normative data request.** Long lead time, blocks Project 2.
3. **Confirm the Connexon item and the signatory question with Ruf** — one message,
   two answers.

---

## Excalidraw Elements

### Required Fields (all elements)
`type`, `id` (unique string), `x`, `y`, `width`, `height`

### Defaults (skip these)
strokeColor="#1e1e1e", backgroundColor="transparent", fillStyle="solid", strokeWidth=2, roughness=1, opacity=100
Canvas background is white.

### Element Types

**Rectangle**: `{ "type": "rectangle", "id": "r1", "x": 100, "y": 100, "width": 200, "height": 100 }`
- `roundness: { type: 3 }` for rounded corners
- `backgroundColor: "#a5d8ff"`, `fillStyle: "solid"` for filled

**Ellipse**: `{ "type": "ellipse", "id": "e1", "x": 100, "y": 100, "width": 150, "height": 150 }`

**Diamond**: `{ "type": "diamond", "id": "d1", "x": 100, "y": 100, "width": 150, "height": 150 }`

**Labeled shape (PREFERRED)**: Add `label` to any shape for auto-centered text. No separate text element needed.
`{ "type": "rectangle", "id": "r1", "x": 100, "y": 100, "width": 200, "height": 80, "label": { "text": "Hello", "fontSize": 20 } }`
- Works on rectangle, ellipse, diamond
- Text auto-centers and container auto-resizes to fit
- Saves tokens vs separate text elements

**Labeled arrow**: `"label": { "text": "connects" }` on an arrow element.

**Standalone text** (titles, annotations only):
`{ "type": "text", "id": "t1", "x": 150, "y": 138, "text": "Hello", "fontSize": 20 }`
- x is the LEFT edge of the text. To center text at position cx: set x = cx - estimatedWidth/2
- estimatedWidth ≈ text.length × fontSize × 0.5
- Do NOT rely on textAlign or width for positioning — they only affect multi-line wrapping

**Arrow**: `{ "type": "arrow", "id": "a1", "x": 300, "y": 150, "width": 200, "height": 0, "points": [[0,0],[200,0]], "endArrowhead": "arrow" }`
- points: [dx, dy] offsets from element x,y
- endArrowhead: null | "arrow" | "bar" | "dot" | "triangle"

### Arrow Bindings
Arrow: `"startBinding": { "elementId": "r1", "fixedPoint": [1, 0.5] }`
fixedPoint: top=[0.5,0], bottom=[0.5,1], left=[0,0.5], right=[1,0.5]

**cameraUpdate** (pseudo-element — controls the viewport, not drawn):
`{ "type": "cameraUpdate", "width": 800, "height": 600, "x": 0, "y": 0 }`
- x, y: top-left corner of the visible area (scene coordinates)
- width, height: size of the visible area — MUST be 4:3 ratio (400×300, 600×450, 800×600, 1200×900, 1600×1200)
- Animates smoothly between positions — use multiple cameraUpdates to guide attention as you draw
- No `id` needed — this is not a drawn element

**delete** (pseudo-element — removes elements by id):
`{ "type": "delete", "ids": "b2,a1,t3" }`
- Comma-separated list of element ids to remove
- Also removes bound text elements (matching `containerId`)
- Place AFTER the elements you want to remove
- Never reuse a deleted id — always assign new ids to replacements

### Drawing Order (CRITICAL for streaming)
- Array order = z-order (first = back, last = front)
- **Emit progressively**: background → shape → its label → its arrows → next shape
- BAD: all rectangles → all texts → all arrows
- GOOD: bg_shape → shape1 → text1 → arrow1 → shape2 → text2 → ...

### Example: Two connected labeled boxes
```json
[
  { "type": "cameraUpdate", "width": 800, "height": 600, "x": 50, "y": 50 },
  { "type": "rectangle", "id": "b1", "x": 100, "y": 100, "width": 200, "height": 100, "roundness": { "type": 3 }, "backgroundColor": "#a5d8ff", "fillStyle": "solid", "label": { "text": "Start", "fontSize": 20 } },
  { "type": "rectangle", "id": "b2", "x": 450, "y": 100, "width": 200, "height": 100, "roundness": { "type": 3 }, "backgroundColor": "#b2f2bb", "fillStyle": "solid", "label": { "text": "End", "fontSize": 20 } },
  { "type": "arrow", "id": "a1", "x": 300, "y": 150, "width": 150, "height": 0, "points": [[0,0],[150,0]], "endArrowhead": "arrow", "startBinding": { "elementId": "b1", "fixedPoint": [1, 0.5] }, "endBinding": { "elementId": "b2", "fixedPoint": [0, 0.5] } }
]
```

### Camera & Sizing (CRITICAL for readability)

The diagram displays inline at ~700px width. Design for this constraint.

**Recommended camera sizes (4:3 aspect ratio ONLY):**
- Camera **S**: width 400, height 300 — close-up on a small group (2-3 elements)
- Camera **M**: width 600, height 450 — medium view, a section of a diagram
- Camera **L**: width 800, height 600 — standard full diagram (DEFAULT)
- Camera **XL**: width 1200, height 900 — large diagram overview. WARNING: font size smaller than 18 is unreadable
- Camera **XXL**: width 1600, height 1200 — panorama / final overview of complex diagrams. WARNING: minimum readable font size is 21

ALWAYS use one of these exact sizes. Non-4:3 viewports cause distortion.

**Font size rules:**
- Minimum fontSize: **16** for body text, labels, descriptions
- Minimum fontSize: **20** for titles and headings
- Minimum fontSize: **14** for secondary annotations only (sparingly)
- NEVER use fontSize below 14 — it becomes unreadable at display scale

**Element sizing rules:**
- Minimum shape size: 120×60 for labeled rectangles/ellipses
- Leave 20-30px gaps between elements minimum
- Prefer fewer, larger elements over many tiny ones

ALWAYS start with a `cameraUpdate` as the FIRST element. For example:
`{ "type": "cameraUpdate", "width": 800, "height": 600, "x": 0, "y": 0 }`

- x, y: top-left corner of visible area (scene coordinates)
- ALWAYS emit the cameraUpdate BEFORE drawing the elements it frames — camera moves first, then content appears
- The camera animates smoothly between positions
- Leave padding: don't match camera size to content size exactly (e.g., 500px content in 800x600 camera)

Examples:
`{ "type": "cameraUpdate", "width": 800, "height": 600, "x": 0, "y": 0 }` — standard view
`{ "type": "cameraUpdate", "width": 400, "height": 300, "x": 200, "y": 100 }` — zoom into a detail
`{ "type": "cameraUpdate", "width": 1600, "height": 1200, "x": -50, "y": -50 }` — panorama overview

Tip: For large diagrams, emit a cameraUpdate to focus on each section as you draw it.

  {"type":"cameraUpdate","width":800,"height":600,"x":-5,"y":2}

## Checkpoints (restoring previous state)

Every create_view call returns a `checkpointId` in its response. To continue from a previous diagram state, start your elements array with a restoreCheckpoint element:

`[{"type":"restoreCheckpoint","id":"<checkpointId>"}, ...additional new elements...]`

The saved state (including any user edits made in fullscreen) is loaded from the client, and your new elements are appended on top. This saves tokens — you don't need to re-send the entire diagram.

## Deleting Elements

Remove elements by id using the `delete` pseudo-element:

`{"type":"delete","ids":"b2,a1,t3"}`

Works in two modes:
- **With restoreCheckpoint**: restore a saved state, then surgically remove specific elements before adding new ones
- **Inline (animation mode)**: draw elements, then delete and replace them later in the same array to create transformation effects

Place delete entries AFTER the elements you want to remove. The final render filters them out.

**IMPORTANT**: Every element id must be unique. Never reuse an id after deleting it — always assign a new id to replacement elements.

## Animation Mode — Transform in Place

Instead of building left-to-right and panning away, you can animate by DELETING elements and replacing them at the same position. Combined with slight camera moves, this creates smooth visual transformations during streaming.

Pattern:
1. Draw initial elements
2. cameraUpdate (shift/zoom slightly)
3. `{"type":"delete","ids":"old1,old2"}`
4. Draw replacements at same coordinates (different color/content)
5. Repeat

Example prompt: "Pixel snake eats apple"

Snake moves right by adding a head segment and deleting the tail. On eating the apple, tail is NOT deleted (snake grows). Camera nudges between frames add subtle motion.

## Dark Mode

If the user asks for a dark theme/mode diagram, use a massive dark background rectangle as the FIRST element (before cameraUpdate). Make it 10x the camera size so it covers the entire viewport even when panning:

`{"type":"rectangle","id":"darkbg","x":-4000,"y":-3000,"width":10000,"height":7500,"backgroundColor":"#1e1e2e","fillStyle":"solid","strokeColor":"transparent","strokeWidth":0}`

Then use these colors on the dark background:

**Text colors (on dark):**
| Color | Hex | Use |
|-------|-----|-----|
| White | `#e5e5e5` | Primary text, titles |
| Muted | `#a0a0a0` | Secondary text, annotations |
| NEVER | `#555` or darker | Invisible on dark bg! |

**Shape fills (on dark):**
| Color | Hex | Good For |
|-------|-----|----------|
| Dark Blue | `#1e3a5f` | Primary nodes |
| Dark Green | `#1a4d2e` | Success, output |
| Dark Purple | `#2d1b69` | Processing, special |
| Dark Orange | `#5c3d1a` | Warning, pending |
| Dark Red | `#5c1a1a` | Error, critical |
| Dark Teal | `#1a4d4d` | Storage, data |

**Stroke/arrow colors (on dark):**
Use the Primary Colors from above — they're bright enough on dark backgrounds. For shape borders, use slightly lighter variants or `#555555` for subtle outlines.

## Tips
- Do NOT call read_me again — you already have everything you need
- Use the color palette consistently
- **Text contrast is CRITICAL** — never use light gray (#b0b0b0, #999) on white backgrounds. Minimum text color on white: #757575. For colored text on light fills, use dark variants (#15803d not #22c55e, #2563eb not #4a9eed). White text needs dark backgrounds (#9a5030 not #c4795b)
- Do NOT use emoji in text — they don't render in Excalidraw's font
- cameraUpdate is MAGICAL and users love it! please use it a lot to guide the user's attention as you draw. It makes a huge difference in readability and engagement.

## Excalidraw Elements

### Required Fields (all elements)
`type`, `id` (unique string), `x`, `y`, `width`, `height`

### Defaults (skip these)
strokeColor="#1e1e1e", backgroundColor="transparent", fillStyle="solid", strokeWidth=2, roughness=1, opacity=100
Canvas background is white.

### Element Types

**Rectangle**: `{ "type": "rectangle", "id": "r1", "x": 100, "y": 100, "width": 200, "height": 100 }`
- `roundness: { type: 3 }` for rounded corners
- `backgroundColor: "#a5d8ff"`, `fillStyle: "solid"` for filled

**Ellipse**: `{ "type": "ellipse", "id": "e1", "x": 100, "y": 100, "width": 150, "height": 150 }`

**Diamond**: `{ "type": "diamond", "id": "d1", "x": 100, "y": 100, "width": 150, "height": 150 }`

**Labeled shape (PREFERRED)**: Add `label` to any shape for auto-centered text. No separate text element needed.
`{ "type": "rectangle", "id": "r1", "x": 100, "y": 100, "width": 200, "height": 80, "label": { "text": "Hello", "fontSize": 20 } }`
- Works on rectangle, ellipse, diamond
- Text auto-centers and container auto-resizes to fit
- Saves tokens vs separate text elements

**Labeled arrow**: `"label": { "text": "connects" }` on an arrow element.

**Standalone text** (titles, annotations only):
`{ "type": "text", "id": "t1", "x": 150, "y": 138, "text": "Hello", "fontSize": 20 }`
- x is the LEFT edge of the text. To center text at position cx: set x = cx - estimatedWidth/2
- estimatedWidth ≈ text.length × fontSize × 0.5
- Do NOT rely on textAlign or width for positioning — they only affect multi-line wrapping

**Arrow**: `{ "type": "arrow", "id": "a1", "x": 300, "y": 150, "width": 200, "height": 0, "points": [[0,0],[200,0]], "endArrowhead": "arrow" }`
- points: [dx, dy] offsets from element x,y
- endArrowhead: null | "arrow" | "bar" | "dot" | "triangle"

### Arrow Bindings
Arrow: `"startBinding": { "elementId": "r1", "fixedPoint": [1, 0.5] }`
fixedPoint: top=[0.5,0], bottom=[0.5,1], left=[0,0.5], right=[1,0.5]

**cameraUpdate** (pseudo-element — controls the viewport, not drawn):
`{ "type": "cameraUpdate", "width": 800, "height": 600, "x": 0, "y": 0 }`
- x, y: top-left corner of the visible area (scene coordinates)
- width, height: size of the visible area — MUST be 4:3 ratio (400×300, 600×450, 800×600, 1200×900, 1600×1200)
- Animates smoothly between positions — use multiple cameraUpdates to guide attention as you draw
- No `id` needed — this is not a drawn element

**delete** (pseudo-element — removes elements by id):
`{ "type": "delete", "ids": "b2,a1,t3" }`
- Comma-separated list of element ids to remove
- Also removes bound text elements (matching `containerId`)
- Place AFTER the elements you want to remove
- Never reuse a deleted id — always assign new ids to replacements

### Drawing Order (CRITICAL for streaming)
- Array order = z-order (first = back, last = front)
- **Emit progressively**: background → shape → its label → its arrows → next shape
- BAD: all rectangles → all texts → all arrows
- GOOD: bg_shape → shape1 → text1 → arrow1 → shape2 → text2 → ...

### Example: Two connected labeled boxes
```json
[
  { "type": "cameraUpdate", "width": 800, "height": 600, "x": 50, "y": 50 },
  { "type": "rectangle", "id": "b1", "x": 100, "y": 100, "width": 200, "height": 100, "roundness": { "type": 3 }, "backgroundColor": "#a5d8ff", "fillStyle": "solid", "label": { "text": "Start", "fontSize": 20 } },
  { "type": "rectangle", "id": "b2", "x": 450, "y": 100, "width": 200, "height": 100, "roundness": { "type": 3 }, "backgroundColor": "#b2f2bb", "fillStyle": "solid", "label": { "text": "End", "fontSize": 20 } },
  { "type": "arrow", "id": "a1", "x": 300, "y": 150, "width": 150, "height": 0, "points": [[0,0],[150,0]], "endArrowhead": "arrow", "startBinding": { "elementId": "b1", "fixedPoint": [1, 0.5] }, "endBinding": { "elementId": "b2", "fixedPoint": [0, 0.5] } }
]
```

### Camera & Sizing (CRITICAL for readability)

The diagram displays inline at ~700px width. Design for this constraint.

**Recommended camera sizes (4:3 aspect ratio ONLY):**
- Camera **S**: width 400, height 300 — close-up on a small group (2-3 elements)
- Camera **M**: width 600, height 450 — medium view, a section of a diagram
- Camera **L**: width 800, height 600 — standard full diagram (DEFAULT)
- Camera **XL**: width 1200, height 900 — large diagram overview. WARNING: font size smaller than 18 is unreadable
- Camera **XXL**: width 1600, height 1200 — panorama / final overview of complex diagrams. WARNING: minimum readable font size is 21

ALWAYS use one of these exact sizes. Non-4:3 viewports cause distortion.

**Font size rules:**
- Minimum fontSize: **16** for body text, labels, descriptions
- Minimum fontSize: **20** for titles and headings
- Minimum fontSize: **14** for secondary annotations only (sparingly)
- NEVER use fontSize below 14 — it becomes unreadable at display scale

**Element sizing rules:**
- Minimum shape size: 120×60 for labeled rectangles/ellipses
- Leave 20-30px gaps between elements minimum
- Prefer fewer, larger elements over many tiny ones

ALWAYS start with a `cameraUpdate` as the FIRST element. For example:
`{ "type": "cameraUpdate", "width": 800, "height": 600, "x": 0, "y": 0 }`

- x, y: top-left corner of visible area (scene coordinates)
- ALWAYS emit the cameraUpdate BEFORE drawing the elements it frames — camera moves first, then content appears
- The camera animates smoothly between positions
- Leave padding: don't match camera size to content size exactly (e.g., 500px content in 800x600 camera)

Examples:
`{ "type": "cameraUpdate", "width": 800, "height": 600, "x": 0, "y": 0 }` — standard view
`{ "type": "cameraUpdate", "width": 400, "height": 300, "x": 200, "y": 100 }` — zoom into a detail
`{ "type": "cameraUpdate", "width": 1600, "height": 1200, "x": -50, "y": -50 }` — panorama overview

Tip: For large diagrams, emit a cameraUpdate to focus on each section as you draw it.

- **Elements overlap when y-coordinates are close** — always check that text, boxes, and labels don't stack on top of each other (e.g., an output box overlapping a zone label)

## Sequence flow Diagram Example

Example prompt: "show a sequence diagram explaining MCP Apps"

This demonstrates a UML-style sequence diagram with 4 actors (User, Agent, App iframe, MCP Server), dashed lifelines, and labeled arrows showing the full MCP Apps request/response flow. Camera pans progressively across the diagram:

- **Camera 1** (600x450): Title "MCP Apps — Sequence Flow"

## Checkpoints (restoring previous state)

Every create_view call returns a `checkpointId` in its response. To continue from a previous diagram state, start your elements array with a restoreCheckpoint element:

`[{"type":"restoreCheckpoint","id":"<checkpointId>"}, ...additional new elements...]`

The saved state (including any user edits made in fullscreen) is loaded from the client, and your new elements are appended on top. This saves tokens — you don't need to re-send the entire diagram.

## Deleting Elements

Remove elements by id using the `delete` pseudo-element:

`{"type":"delete","ids":"b2,a1,t3"}`

Works in two modes:
- **With restoreCheckpoint**: restore a saved state, then surgically remove specific elements before adding new ones
- **Inline (animation mode)**: draw elements, then delete and replace them later in the same array to create transformation effects

Place delete entries AFTER the elements you want to remove. The final render filters them out.

**IMPORTANT**: Every element id must be unique. Never reuse an id after deleting it — always assign a new id to replacement elements.

## Animation Mode — Transform in Place

Instead of building left-to-right and panning away, you can animate by DELETING elements and replacing them at the same position. Combined with slight camera moves, this creates smooth visual transformations during streaming.

Pattern:
1. Draw initial elements
2. cameraUpdate (shift/zoom slightly)
3. `{"type":"delete","ids":"old1,old2"}`
4. Draw replacements at same coordinates (different color/content)
5. Repeat

Example prompt: "Pixel snake eats apple"

Snake moves right by adding a head segment and deleting the tail. On eating the apple, tail is NOT deleted (snake grows). Camera nudges between frames add subtle motion.

## Dark Mode

If the user asks for a dark theme/mode diagram, use a massive dark background rectangle as the FIRST element (before cameraUpdate). Make it 10x the camera size so it covers the entire viewport even when panning:

**Stroke/arrow colors (on dark):**
Use the Primary Colors from above — they're bright enough on dark backgrounds. For shape borders, use slightly lighter variants or `#555555` for subtle outlines.

## Tips
- Do NOT call read_me again — you already have everything you need
- Use the color palette consistently
- **Text contrast is CRITICAL** — never use light gray (#b0b0b0, #999) on white backgrounds. Minimum text color on white: #757575. For colored text on light fills, use dark variants (#15803d not #22c55e, #2563eb not #4a9eed). White text needs dark backgrounds (#9a5030 not #c4795b)

# Applied Performance — Project Execution Plan
## Linda Mungai, Applied Performance Specialist
### 2026–27

Prepared 2026-08-19 · Supervisor: Eric Rash, Director of Applied Performance

---

## How to read this

Four projects. Each one moves through the same three phases:

**IDEATION** → what are we building and is it possible
**DEVELOPMENT** → build it, test it, break it, fix it
**COMPLETION** → deliver the artifact and write up what happened

Every project ends in a **written artifact**. That is deliberate. Work that leaves
nothing behind is hard to point at later, and you have periodic progress reports to
file. Each completed milestone below is one line you can use in those reports.

**Dates are months, not deadlines.** Sport schedules move. The order matters more than
the calendar — some milestones are gates, and the work after a gate does not start until
the gate is passed.

---

## Master tracker

Update the status column at each supervision meeting. That is the whole tracking system.

| # | Project | Phase | Status | Target |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **P1** | Women's tennis performance profiles | Ideation | Not started | Sept |
| | | Development | Not started | Sept–Oct |
| | | Completion | Not started | Oct–Nov |
| **P2** | Normative ranges | Ideation | Not started | Sept–Oct |
| | | Development | Not started | Nov–Jan |
| | | Completion | Not started | Jan–Feb |
| **P3** | Tennis conditioning test (R&D) | Ideation | Not started | Oct–Dec |
| | | Development | Not started | Jan–Mar |
| | | Completion | Not started | Mar–May |
| **P4** | Match profiles | Ideation (gate) | Not started | Jan–Feb |
| | | Development | Not started | Feb–Apr |
| | | Completion | Not started | Apr–May |

**Status codes:** Not started · In progress · Blocked · Done

Use **Blocked** freely and early. A blocked milestone that gets said out loud in week two
is a scheduling problem. The same one found in month five is a dead project.

---

## Dependencies — what waits on what

```
P1 (profiles) ──────> P2 (normative ranges)
                              │
P3 (conditioning test) ───────┼──────> P4 (match profiles)
                              │
                     [data feasibility gate]
```

- **P2 cannot start** before P1 has produced data. You cannot norm what you have not measured.
- **P4 cannot start** before P1 and P3 exist, and before the data feasibility gate passes.
- **P3 runs independently** of P1 and P2. It is the one you can push on when tennis testing is blocked by the schedule.

---

# P1 — Women's tennis performance profiles

**In one line:** every woman on the roster gets a neuromuscular profile built from force
plate, ForceFrame, and NordBord testing.

**Why this one is first:** small squad, low friction, and it produces the raw data that
P2 and P4 both need. Nothing else starts properly until this exists.

### Ideation — September

| | Milestone | Done when |
|---|---|---|
| ☐ | **1.1** Equipment audit | Written list of every device, where it lives, and its last calibration date. Anything uncalibrated is flagged before, not after, testing. |
| ☐ | **1.2** Lock the test battery | A written protocol exists and Eric has signed off: which tests, in what order, warm-up, reps, rest, coaching cues, and the exact data fields captured. |
| ☐ | **1.3** Schedule the testing window | Dates on TeamUp, confirmed with Blair and the coaching staff. |

> **Lock the protocol before the first athlete is tested.** If the battery changes
> mid-year, every comparison across time becomes meaningless and the profiles are worth
> nothing. This is a one-way door. Take the extra week here.

### Development — September–October

| | Milestone | Done when |
|---|---|---|
| ☐ | **1.4** Pilot on 2–3 athletes | Full run-through completed end to end. The protocol is revised wherever it broke — and it will break somewhere. |
| ☐ | **1.5** Test the full roster | Every athlete has a complete data set. No missing fields. Missing data found now is fixable; found in December it is not. |
| ☐ | **1.6** Build the profile template | A one-page per-athlete sheet that populates from the export rather than being retyped by hand. |

### Completion — October–November

| | Milestone | Done when |
|---|---|---|
| ☐ | **1.7** Profiles delivered | Every athlete has a profile sheet and the staff has seen them. |
| ☐ | **1.8** Written summary | 1–2 pages: what the battery is, what it found, what happens next. |

**Artifacts produced:** testing protocol · per-athlete profile sheets · summary write-up

---

# P2 — Normative ranges

**In one line:** turn the P1 data into reference ranges — what is normal for our women,
and how that compares to the wider collegiate picture.

**Why it matters:** a number with no reference range is not information. This is the
project that makes P1 usable by somebody who is not you.

### Ideation — September–October

| | Milestone | Done when |
|---|---|---|
| ☐ | **2.1** Request the VALD collegiate comparison data | Request sent and logged. **Do this in September** — the lead time is long and it blocks the back half of this project. |
| ☐ | **2.2** Decide which variables get normed | A short, agreed list. Resist norming everything; pick the variables that would actually change a decision. |

### Development — November–January

| | Milestone | Done when |
|---|---|---|
| ☐ | **2.3** Establish the noise floor — **GATE** | Typical error (TE) and smallest worthwhile change (SWC) calculated and written down for every variable being normed. |
| ☐ | **2.4** Build the analysis in Python | A script that takes the raw export and outputs the ranges. Re-runnable next year without rebuilding it. |
| ☐ | **2.5** Build the internal ranges | Banded ranges per variable, with the sample size and spread stated on the page. |

> **2.3 is a hard gate, and it is the most important line in this document.**
>
> Establish the measurement error *before* you interpret whether anyone's score is high
> or low. If you skip it, you will confidently tell a coach an athlete has declined when
> what actually happened is the test wobbled. That mistake is invisible, it is common,
> and it destroys trust permanently once someone works it out.
>
> Rule of thumb: if a change is smaller than the typical error of the test, you cannot
> claim the change is real. Say "we can't tell" — it is a better answer than a wrong one.
>
> Use `tools/reliability.py` in the AgentAssist repo. Don't compute this by hand or by
> eye. Ask Eric to walk you through it the first time.

### Completion — January–February

| | Milestone | Done when |
|---|---|---|
| ☐ | **2.6** Benchmark against collegiate data | Comparison table, with the caveats written directly onto it — different populations, different protocols, different equipment. |
| ☐ | **2.7** Reference sheet delivered | One-page ranges sheet, plus the script saved somewhere the staff can find and re-run it. |

**Artifacts produced:** reliability write-up (TE/SWC) · Python analysis script · normative reference sheet

---

# P3 — Tennis-specific conditioning test (R&D)

**In one line:** research, design, present, and pilot a conditioning test built for tennis.

**Why it is the flagship:** it is the only project with a full research arc, and it
produces three separate artifacts. It is also the one most likely to be interesting to
talk about later. Give it real time.

**Set expectations with yourself early:** the value here is the research and the design
work. If the test is not adopted this year, that is a normal outcome for applied research
in a coaching environment. A well-built test that nobody runs yet is still a completed
project. Do not measure this one by whether a coach says yes.

### Ideation — October–December

| | Milestone | Done when |
|---|---|---|
| ☐ | **3.1** Literature review | 8–12 sources summarized. Each one rated for whether it is actually feasible with our equipment, our court time, and our squad size. Feasibility is the column that matters. |
| ☐ | **3.2** Shortlist 2–3 candidate models | Written comparison — pros, cons, equipment needed, time cost, what it actually measures. |

### Development — January–March

| | Milestone | Done when |
|---|---|---|
| ☐ | **3.3** Draft the protocol | Full written protocol: heart rate setup, timing gate positions, scoring, and a **test-retest reliability plan built in from the start**. |
| ☐ | **3.4** Present to applied performance staff | Presented at a biweekly staff meeting. Feedback written down. Internal first — always. |
| ☐ | **3.5** Present to tennis staff | Routed through Blair. Decision recorded either way, yes or no. |

> **Pair the conditioning test with a jump test, before and after.** Run a force plate
> jump immediately pre and post. That gives you neuromuscular fatigue measured against
> cardiovascular load in the same session — which is a genuinely interesting question and
> sits squarely in your background. It costs about four extra minutes and roughly doubles
> what the project is worth.

### Completion — March–May

| | Milestone | Done when |
|---|---|---|
| ☐ | **3.6** Pilot the test | Run **twice** on a willing group — a single run tells you nothing about reliability. |
| ☐ | **3.7** Results report | Written report: reliability numbers, what the test showed, and a clear recommendation to keep, change, or drop it. "Drop it, here's why" is a valid and respectable finding. |

**Artifacts produced:** literature review · test protocol · pilot results report

---

# P4 — Match profiles

**In one line:** connect what happens on court to what we see in the weight room and in
conditioning.

**This project starts with a gate, not with work.**

### Ideation — January–February

| | Milestone | Done when |
|---|---|---|
| ☐ | **4.1** Data feasibility check — **GATE** | A written yes/no: what match data exists, who owns it, whether we can get it, and in what format. |
| ☐ | **4.2** Define the data streams | If 4.1 is yes: name the three streams being joined and the key that joins them. |

> **If 4.1 comes back no, this project stops and that is a clean result — not a failure.**
> Write the one-page feasibility finding, file it, and put the hours into P3. Knowing that
> the data is not accessible is itself useful to the department, and a written negative
> finding is a real deliverable. Do not spend three months trying to force it.

### Development — February–April

| | Milestone | Done when |
|---|---|---|
| ☐ | **4.3** Pull and join the data | Match data joined to weight-room and conditioning data, with a written note on every assumption the join required. |
| ☐ | **4.4** Build 2 pilot profiles | Two athletes profiled end to end before scaling to the roster. |

### Completion — April–May

| | Milestone | Done when |
|---|---|---|
| ☐ | **4.5** Holistic athlete report | A per-athlete report joining on-court demand, weight-room output, and conditioning response. |

**Artifacts produced:** feasibility finding · joined dataset with documented assumptions · holistic athlete reports

---

# Ongoing threads

These run continuously rather than in phases. They are not projects, but they are real work.

### Load monitoring and wellness — women's tennis

The high/low model is already partly in place: denser work Monday/Wednesday/Friday,
regen and mobility Tuesday/Thursday. Your job is to **measure what is already
happening**, not to redesign it.

Start small and boring: session RPE plus a short wellness check. Something a whole squad
will actually complete every day beats something elegant that they complete for two weeks.

**Monthly:** one-page trend summary to Eric.

### Athlete education

Own **one topic end to end** rather than assisting on five. Pick something in your
wheelhouse — sleep, fatigue, recovery, or how the nervous system responds to training
load. Build it once, deliver it, keep it.

**Target:** one delivered session per semester.

---

# How this gets tracked

**Every two weeks — supervision meeting with Eric.**

Bring three things:

1. The master tracker, updated
2. Anything marked **Blocked**, and what would unblock it
3. One thing you learned

That is the whole meeting. Fifteen minutes if nothing is on fire.

**After each meeting, add two lines to a running log:** what moved, what is next.

Do this even when it feels like nothing happened — especially then. You have periodic
progress reports to submit against your training plan, and reconstructing a year from
memory the week they are due is how those reports end up thin. Two lines every two weeks
means the report writes itself.

**Every completed milestone in this document is one line in that report.** There are 25
of them. You will not be short of material.

---

# Ground rules

**Data privacy.** Athlete data is FERPA-covered and may be HIPAA-covered. It is **not**
covered by Baylor's AI approval.

- Spreadsheets, Python scripts, local analysis on identifiable athlete data: **fine.**
- Pasting athlete names, rosters, or identifiable performance data into ChatGPT, Claude,
  or any AI tool: **not fine.** No exceptions, no "just to check the formatting."

If a task seems to need identifiable data in an AI tool, stop and ask Eric. There is
almost always another way.

**Nothing goes to a coach unreviewed.** Every analysis, report, and recommendation goes
through Eric before it reaches a coaching staff. This is not a comment on your judgement
— it is how the department works and it protects you as much as anyone.

**Ask early.** A question in week one costs five minutes. The same question in month
three costs a rebuild.

# Applied Performance — Project Execution Plan
## Linda Mungai, Applied Performance Specialist
### 2026–27

Prepared 2026-08-19 · Supervisor: Eric Rash, Director of Applied Performance

---

## How to read this

Four projects. Each one moves through the same three phases:

**IDEATION** → what are we building and is it possible
**DEVELOPMENT** → build it, test it, break it, fix it
**COMPLETION** → deliver the artifact and write up what happened

Every project ends in a **written artifact**. That is deliberate. Work that leaves
nothing behind is hard to point at later, and you have periodic progress reports to
file. Each completed milestone below is one line you can use in those reports.

**Dates are months, not deadlines.** Sport schedules move. The order matters more than
the calendar — some milestones are gates, and the work after a gate does not start until
the gate is passed.

---

## Master tracker

Update the status column at each supervision meeting. That is the whole tracking system.

| # | Project | Phase | Status | Target |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **P1** | Women's tennis performance profiles | Ideation | Not started | Sept |
| | | Development | Not started | Sept–Oct |
| | | Completion | Not started | Oct–Nov |
| **P2** | Normative ranges | Ideation | Not started | Sept–Oct |
| | | Development | Not started | Nov–Jan |
| | | Completion | Not started | Jan–Feb |
| **P3** | Tennis conditioning test (R&D) | Ideation | Not started | Oct–Dec |
| | | Development | Not started | Jan–Mar |
| | | Completion | Not started | Mar–May |
| **P4** | Match profiles | Ideation (gate) | Not started | Jan–Feb |
| | | Development | Not started | Feb–Apr |
| | | Completion | Not started | Apr–May |

**Status codes:** Not started · In progress · Blocked · Done

Use **Blocked** freely and early. A blocked milestone that gets said out loud in week two
is a scheduling problem. The same one found in month five is a dead project.

---

## Dependencies — what waits on what

```
P1 (profiles) ──────> P2 (normative ranges)
                              │
P3 (conditioning test) ───────┼──────> P4 (match profiles)
                              │
                     [data feasibility gate]
```

- **P2 cannot start** before P1 has produced data. You cannot norm what you have not measured.
- **P4 cannot start** before P1 and P3 exist, and before the data feasibility gate passes.
- **P3 runs independently** of P1 and P2. It is the one you can push on when tennis testing is blocked by the schedule.

---

# P1 — Women's tennis performance profiles

**In one line:** every woman on the roster gets a neuromuscular profile built from force
plate, ForceFrame, and NordBord testing.

**Why this one is first:** small squad, low friction, and it produces the raw data that
P2 and P4 both need. Nothing else starts properly until this exists.

### Ideation — September

| | Milestone | Done when |
|---|---|---|
| ☐ | **1.1** Equipment audit | Written list of every device, where it lives, and its last calibration date. Anything uncalibrated is flagged before, not after, testing. |
| ☐ | **1.2** Lock the test battery | A written protocol exists and Eric has signed off: which tests, in what order, warm-up, reps, rest, coaching cues, and the exact data fields captured. |
| ☐ | **1.3** Schedule the testing window | Dates on TeamUp, confirmed with Blair and the coaching staff. |

> **Lock the protocol before the first athlete is tested.** If the battery changes
> mid-year, every comparison across time becomes meaningless and the profiles are worth
> nothing. This is a one-way door. Take the extra week here.

### Development — September–October

| | Milestone | Done when |
|---|---|---|
| ☐ | **1.4** Pilot on 2–3 athletes | Full run-through completed end to end. The protocol is revised wherever it broke — and it will break somewhere. |
| ☐ | **1.5** Test the full roster | Every athlete has a complete data set. No missing fields. Missing data found now is fixable; found in December it is not. |
| ☐ | **1.6** Build the profile template | A one-page per-athlete sheet that populates from the export rather than being retyped by hand. |

### Completion — October–November

| | Milestone | Done when |
|---|---|---|
| ☐ | **1.7** Profiles delivered | Every athlete has a profile sheet and the staff has seen them. |
| ☐ | **1.8** Written summary | 1–2 pages: what the battery is, what it found, what happens next. |

**Artifacts produced:** testing protocol · per-athlete profile sheets · summary write-up

---

# P2 — Normative ranges

**In one line:** turn the P1 data into reference ranges — what is normal for our women,
and how that compares to the wider collegiate picture.

**Why it matters:** a number with no reference range is not information. This is the
project that makes P1 usable by somebody who is not you.

### Ideation — September–October

| | Milestone | Done when |
|---|---|---|
| ☐ | **2.1** Request the VALD collegiate comparison data | Request sent and logged. **Do this in September** — the lead time is long and it blocks the back half of this project. |
| ☐ | **2.2** Decide which variables get normed | A short, agreed list. Resist norming everything; pick the variables that would actually change a decision. |

### Development — November–January

| | Milestone | Done when |
|---|---|---|
| ☐ | **2.3** Establish the noise floor — **GATE** | Typical error (TE) and smallest worthwhile change (SWC) calculated and written down for every variable being normed. |
| ☐ | **2.4** Build the analysis in Python | A script that takes the raw export and outputs the ranges. Re-runnable next year without rebuilding it. |
| ☐ | **2.5** Build the internal ranges | Banded ranges per variable, with the sample size and spread stated on the page. |

> **2.3 is a hard gate, and it is the most important line in this document.**
>
> Establish the measurement error *before* you interpret whether anyone's score is high
> or low. If you skip it, you will confidently tell a coach an athlete has declined when
> what actually happened is the test wobbled. That mistake is invisible, it is common,
> and it destroys trust permanently once someone works it out.
>
> Rule of thumb: if a change is smaller than the typical error of the test, you cannot
> claim the change is real. Say "we can't tell" — it is a better answer than a wrong one.
>
> Use `tools/reliability.py` in the AgentAssist repo. Don't compute this by hand or by
> eye. Ask Eric to walk you through it the first time.

### Completion — January–February

| | Milestone | Done when |
|---|---|---|
| ☐ | **2.6** Benchmark against collegiate data | Comparison table, with the caveats written directly onto it — different populations, different protocols, different equipment. |
| ☐ | **2.7** Reference sheet delivered | One-page ranges sheet, plus the script saved somewhere the staff can find and re-run it. |

**Artifacts produced:** reliability write-up (TE/SWC) · Python analysis script · normative reference sheet

---

# P3 — Tennis-specific conditioning test (R&D)

**In one line:** research, design, present, and pilot a conditioning test built for tennis.

**Why it is the flagship:** it is the only project with a full research arc, and it
produces three separate artifacts. It is also the one most likely to be interesting to
talk about later. Give it real time.

**Set expectations with yourself early:** the value here is the research and the design
work. If the test is not adopted this year, that is a normal outcome for applied research
in a coaching environment. A well-built test that nobody runs yet is still a completed
project. Do not measure this one by whether a coach says yes.

### Ideation — October–December

| | Milestone | Done when |
|---|---|---|
| ☐ | **3.1** Literature review | 8–12 sources summarized. Each one rated for whether it is actually feasible with our equipment, our court time, and our squad size. Feasibility is the column that matters. |
| ☐ | **3.2** Shortlist 2–3 candidate models | Written comparison — pros, cons, equipment needed, time cost, what it actually measures. |

### Development — January–March

| | Milestone | Done when |
|---|---|---|
| ☐ | **3.3** Draft the protocol | Full written protocol: heart rate setup, timing gate positions, scoring, and a **test-retest reliability plan built in from the start**. |
| ☐ | **3.4** Present to applied performance staff | Presented at a biweekly staff meeting. Feedback written down. Internal first — always. |
| ☐ | **3.5** Present to tennis staff | Routed through Blair. Decision recorded either way, yes or no. |

> **Pair the conditioning test with a jump test, before and after.** Run a force plate
> jump immediately pre and post. That gives you neuromuscular fatigue measured against
> cardiovascular load in the same session — which is a genuinely interesting question and
> sits squarely in your background. It costs about four extra minutes and roughly doubles
> what the project is worth.

### Completion — March–May

| | Milestone | Done when |
|---|---|---|
| ☐ | **3.6** Pilot the test | Run **twice** on a willing group — a single run tells you nothing about reliability. |
| ☐ | **3.7** Results report | Written report: reliability numbers, what the test showed, and a clear recommendation to keep, change, or drop it. "Drop it, here's why" is a valid and respectable finding. |

**Artifacts produced:** literature review · test protocol · pilot results report

---

# P4 — Match profiles

**In one line:** connect what happens on court to what we see in the weight room and in
conditioning.

**This project starts with a gate, not with work.**

### Ideation — January–February

| | Milestone | Done when |
|---|---|---|
| ☐ | **4.1** Data feasibility check — **GATE** | A written yes/no: what match data exists, who owns it, whether we can get it, and in what format. |
| ☐ | **4.2** Define the data streams | If 4.1 is yes: name the three streams being joined and the key that joins them. |

> **If 4.1 comes back no, this project stops and that is a clean result — not a failure.**
> Write the one-page feasibility finding, file it, and put the hours into P3. Knowing that
> the data is not accessible is itself useful to the department, and a written negative
> finding is a real deliverable. Do not spend three months trying to force it.

### Development — February–April

| | Milestone | Done when |
|---|---|---|
| ☐ | **4.3** Pull and join the data | Match data joined to weight-room and conditioning data, with a written note on every assumption the join required. |
| ☐ | **4.4** Build 2 pilot profiles | Two athletes profiled end to end before scaling to the roster. |

### Completion — April–May

| | Milestone | Done when |
|---|---|---|
| ☐ | **4.5** Holistic athlete report | A per-athlete report joining on-court demand, weight-room output, and conditioning response. |

**Artifacts produced:** feasibility finding · joined dataset with documented assumptions · holistic athlete reports

---

# Ongoing threads

These run continuously rather than in phases. They are not projects, but they are real work.

### Load monitoring and wellness — women's tennis

The high/low model is already partly in place: denser work Monday/Wednesday/Friday,
regen and mobility Tuesday/Thursday. Your job is to **measure what is already
happening**, not to redesign it.

Start small and boring: session RPE plus a short wellness check. Something a whole squad
will actually complete every day beats something elegant that they complete for two weeks.

**Monthly:** one-page trend summary to Eric.

### Athlete education

Own **one topic end to end** rather than assisting on five. Pick something in your
wheelhouse — sleep, fatigue, recovery, or how the nervous system responds to training
load. Build it once, deliver it, keep it.

**Target:** one delivered session per semester.

---

# How this gets tracked

**Every two weeks — supervision meeting with Eric.**

Bring three things:

1. The master tracker, updated
2. Anything marked **Blocked**, and what would unblock it
3. One thing you learned

That is the whole meeting. Fifteen minutes if nothing is on fire.

**After each meeting, add two lines to a running log:** what moved, what is next.

Do this even when it feels like nothing happened — especially then. You have periodic
progress reports to submit against your training plan, and reconstructing a year from
memory the week they are due is how those reports end up thin. Two lines every two weeks
means the report writes itself.

**Every completed milestone in this document is one line in that report.** There are 25
of them. You will not be short of material.

---

# Ground rules

**Data privacy.** Athlete data is FERPA-covered and may be HIPAA-covered. It is **not**
covered by Baylor's AI approval.

- Spreadsheets, Python scripts, local analysis on identifiable athlete data: **fine.**
- Pasting athlete names, rosters, or identifiable performance data into ChatGPT, Claude,
  or any AI tool: **not fine.** No exceptions, no "just to check the formatting."

If a task seems to need identifiable data in an AI tool, stop and ask Eric. There is
almost always another way.

**Nothing goes to a coach unreviewed.** Every analysis, report, and recommendation goes
through Eric before it reaches a coaching staff. This is not a comment on your judgement
— it is how the department works and it protects you as much as anyone.

**Ask early.** A question in week one costs five minutes. The same question in month
three costs a rebuild.

---

2. **Draft the test battery protocol (1.2).** Bring the draft to your first supervision

3. **Send the VALD data request (2.1).** Long lead time. Sending it in September costs
   nothing and buys three months.

## Step 2 — Verify the artifacts match

For each decided/promised item, check the actual artifact — not the conversation:

- `git log --since="<last meeting date>"` in the project repo to see what actually shipped.
- Note any artifact that is stale, locked, or missing.

Mark each item ✅ implemented / ⚠️ partially / ❌ not reflected.

## Step 3 — The brief

```
## Meeting Prep — <project> (<meeting date/person if known>)

**Bottom line:** ready / ready with caveats / gaps found

✅ <decision> — in <file path>

**Bring up in the meeting:** <open questions, items awaiting their input>

**Deliverables & paths:** <every file they might present or reference, full paths>
```

# Meeting run sheet — Linda Mungai
## Thursday 2026-08-20 · Project kickoff

**ERIC ONLY.** This file contains a do-not-say list. Do not hand this one over.

---

## Before you walk in

**Bring:** printed copy of `04_Linda_OnePager.md` for her. That is the only thing she
takes away today.

**Do not hand her `01_ExecutionPlan_LindaFacing.md` in this meeting.** It is 27
milestones and it is correct, but it is a reference document, not a first-meeting
document. Send it after, once she has the shape in her head. If she asks for detail in
the room, tell her the full plan is coming by email — that is a good answer.

**Never `02_...CONFIDENTIAL.md`.** That one is yours permanently.

---

## Timing

Built as a **30-minute core**. Items marked *if time* are the stretch. If you get cut to
15, run blocks 1, 2, and 5 and skip the rest — the two decisions in block 5 are the only
things that genuinely must happen today.

---

## The agenda

### 1 · Frame the year — 5 min

Four projects, September to May. Each one moves the same way: work out what we're
building, build it, hand it over with something written down.

The line worth saying out loud: **a project is finished when there is a document, not
when the work stops.** Say it once here and you will not have to enforce it later.

Reason it matters to her specifically: she has periodic progress reports to file against
her training plan. Every finished milestone is a line she can use. Framing the paperwork
as a by-product of good work — rather than as extra work — is the single most useful
thing you can do for her in this meeting.

### 2 · Walk the four projects — 10 min

Use the one-pager. Do not go milestone by milestone.

- **P1 Profiles** *(Sept–Nov)* — starts now, feeds everything else
- **P2 Norms** *(Sept–Feb)* — turns P1 into something a coach can read
- **P3 Conditioning test** *(Oct–May)* — the flagship, the one with a real research arc
- **P4 Match profiles** *(Jan–May)* — opens with a data-access check

Two things to land, and only two:

> **P1 has a one-way door.** The test battery gets locked in writing before anyone is
> tested. Change it in January and every comparison across the year is worthless. This is
> why the first month looks slow.

> **P3 is complete either way.** If the coaching staff runs the test, great. If they
> don't, she still writes the report and the project is still done. Say this *now*,
> before she is invested — it is much less convincing said in March.

### 3 · How we work together — 5 min

- **Every two weeks, 15 minutes.** She brings the tracker, anything blocked, and one
  thing she learned.
- **Say "blocked" early.** Week two it's a scheduling problem. Month five it's a dead
  project.
- **Nothing goes to a coach unreviewed.** Frame it as how the department works and as
  cover for her, not as a comment on her judgement — she is new and will hear it wrong
  otherwise.
- **Athlete data never goes into an AI tool.** Names, rosters, identifiable performance
  data — not into ChatGPT, Claude, anything. Local scripts and spreadsheets are fine. Say
  this plainly; it is not obvious and it is the one that gets people in real trouble.

### 4 · Questions for her — 7 min

This half matters. Do not let the meeting be you talking for 30 minutes.

- **How much Python has she actually written?** P2 assumes she writes the analysis
  herself. If the honest answer is "not much," the project still works — it just needs
  more runway and a check-in on it. Better to know tomorrow than in November.
- **How familiar is she with force plates, ForceFrame, NordBord?** Has she run a testing
  session on her own before?
- **What does her week actually look like?** She has real duties on top of this —
  onboarding lead, community service, the tennis schedule, men's tennis cover when Hobby
  travels. Find out where the hours are before assuming they exist.
- **What does she think of the test battery?** Genuinely ask. She may have seen a better
  protocol, and asking now buys ownership later.
- **Anything she wants to work on that isn't on this list?**

### 5 · Two decisions to land — 3 min

**Do not leave the room without these.**

1. **Put the recurring supervision meeting on both calendars.** Now, in the room, phones
   out. It is a requirement of her training plan and it is still not scheduled. It will
   not happen by intention alone.
2. **Pick a date for the equipment audit (milestone 1.1).** Concrete, an afternoon's
   work, and it will surface at least one surprise. It gives her something real to do
   before the next meeting.

### 6 · Ask her for the full form — 1 min

You hold **pages 3 and 5 only** of her I-983. Pages 1, 2, and 4 are missing. She filed
it — she almost certainly has the complete copy. One sentence, easy ask, closes the gap.

While you are there, confirm with her: what are the actual due dates on her progress
evaluations? She will know, or she knows who to ask.

### 7 · *If time*

- Load monitoring and wellness for tennis — measure what is already happening, do not
  redesign it
- Athlete education — she owns **one** topic end to end, not five as an assistant
- The biweekly applied performance staff meeting — she is expected there

---

## Do not say

Three things from `02_...CONFIDENTIAL.md` stay out of this room:

| Do not say | Say instead |
|---|---|
| That Ruf expects Joey to ignore the conditioning test | "Getting it adopted isn't the measure — the research and the report are." |
| That authority with coaches comes from Chris and Kenny, not you | "If a coach conversation needs more weight behind it, bring it to me and I'll handle the routing." |
| That P4 is the project you would cut first | "P4 opens with a data-access check. If the data isn't there, we write that up and stop — that's a clean result." |

**Her own visa and OPT situation is fine to discuss with her.** It is her application and
her form. The three items above are about other people, and that is the difference.

---

## Also keep off her agenda

These are Ruf's to answer, not hers:

- Whether the Connexon / volleyball analysis is hers or Blair's
- Who signs the progress evaluations, you or Kenny

Chase both with Ruf separately.

---

|---|---|---|---|

Plus two ongoing threads: **load monitoring and wellness** for women's tennis, and

---

## The shape of the year

| | Sep | Oct | Nov | Dec | Jan | Feb | Mar | Apr | May |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **P1** | Ideate | Build | Deliver | | | | | | |
| **P2** | Ideate | Ideate | Build | Build | Build | Deliver | | | |
| **P3** | | Ideate | Ideate | Ideate | Build | Build | Build | Deliver | Deliver |
| **P4** | | | | | Gate | Build | Build | Build | Deliver |

**P2 needs P1's data. P4 needs P1 and P3.** P3 runs independently — it's the one to push
on when tennis testing gets blocked by the schedule.

---

## How every project moves

**Ideation** → what are we building, and can we actually do it
**Development** → build it, pilot it small, fix what broke, run it for real
**Completion** → deliver the artifact, write up what happened

> **A project is finished when there's something written down — not when the work stops.**

---

## Two things that will save you

**Lock the P1 test battery in writing before testing anyone.** If the battery changes
partway through the year, every comparison across time becomes meaningless. This is why
month one looks slow. It isn't slow — it's the part that makes the rest count.

error. If a change is smaller than that error, you can't say the change is real. "We
can't tell yet" is a better answer than a confident wrong one, and it's the answer that
keeps a coach trusting you. We'll walk through the tools for this together.

---

1. The tracker, updated
2. Anything **blocked** — and what would unblock it
3. One thing you learned

a dead project.

After each meeting, two lines in a running log: what moved, what's next. Do it even when
nothing happened — especially then.

---

## Two ground rules

**Nothing goes to a coach unreviewed.** Every analysis and recommendation comes through
Eric first. That's how the department works, and it protects you.

**Athlete data never goes into an AI tool.** Spreadsheets, Python, local analysis — all
fine. Pasting athlete names, rosters, or performance data into ChatGPT, Claude, or
anything similar — not fine, no exceptions. If a task seems to need it, stop and ask.

---

## Your first three things

1. **Equipment audit.** What do we have, where is it, when was it last calibrated?
2. **Draft the test battery protocol.** Bring the draft to our next meeting rather than
   waiting to be told what's in it.
3. **Send the VALD data request.** Long lead time — sending it in September buys three
   months.

---

**Ask early.** A question in week one costs five minutes. The same question in month
three costs a rebuild.
